items.stem: What is a free good?
options: A good with a price of zero in shops
A good that is not scarce and has zero opportunity cost
A good provided by the government without charge
A good given away by firms as a promotion
items.answer: A good that is not scarce and has zero opportunity cost
items.markingKey: Free good: unlimited supply relative to demand; no resources used.

items.stem: What is an economic good?
options: A good that is always produced by the private sector
A good that can only be bought with money
A good that is scarce and so has an opportunity cost
A good that is produced abroad
items.answer: A good that is scarce and so has an opportunity cost
items.markingKey: Economic goods use scarce resources.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a free good and an economic good.
items.answer: A free good is unlimited relative to demand, so no resources are used and the opportunity cost is zero (e.g. sunlight). An economic good is scarce, uses resources and has an opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: free good definition; 1 mark: economic good definition [2]

items.stem: A loaf of bread bought in a supermarket in Nairobi. How is this good best classified?
items.answer: Private good
items.markingKey: Private good: excludable and rivalrous.

items.stem: Extract: The government of Marvona has introduced a 20% tax on sugary drinks and used the revenue to fund free fruit in primary schools and a new public park in Nairobi. The share of adults who drink sugary drinks daily fell from 28% to 24%. Some critics argue that people should be free to choose what they consume. (a) Explain why sugary drinks may be classified as a demerit good. (b) Explain why free fruit in schools may increase economic welfare.
items.answer: (a) Consumers underestimate the long-term health harm, so they over-consume relative to the optimum. (b) Merit good under-consumed due to information failure; free provision raises consumption; long-term health benefits.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Consumers underestimate the long-term health harm, so they over-consume relative to the optimum. [2] (b) Credit: Merit good under-consumed due to information failure; free provision raises consumption; long-term health benefits. [2]

items.stem: Which is a free good?
items.answer: Sunlight
items.markingKey: Abundant, no resources needed, zero opportunity cost.

items.stem: In Zentara, the state supplies drinking water free of charge. Treating and piping water costs $1.2 per 1,000 litres. The population is 3 million and each person uses 150 litres a day. Calculate the annual cost of supplying the water, in millions of dollars.
items.answer: $197.1 million

items.stem: What are the two characteristics of a pure public good?
items.answer: Non-excludable and non-rivalrous
items.markingKey: Non-excludability (cannot stop non-payers) and non-rivalry (use by one does not reduce availability to others).

items.stem: Explain why the free rider problem leads to a missing market for public goods.
items.answer: Because non-payers cannot be excluded, people can benefit without paying, so few are willing to pay; firms cannot earn revenue, so no firm supplies the good.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: non-excludability; 1 mark: free riding/no willingness to pay; 1 mark: no profit, so not provided [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a private good and a public good.
items.answer: Private goods are excludable and rivalrous (e.g. food); public goods are non-excludable and non-rivalrous (e.g. street lighting).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Cigarettes sold in Rovania. How is this good best classified?
items.answer: Demerit good
items.markingKey: Demerit good: more harmful than consumers realise; over-consumed in a free market.

items.answer: Demerit good: more harmful than consumers realise; over-consumed in a free market.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Demerit good; 1 mark: explanation – more harmful than consumers realise; over-consumed in a free market. [2]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by a quasi-public good, using an example.
items.answer: A good with some but not all public-good characteristics, e.g. a road is largely non-rivalrous until congested, and exclusion is possible with tolls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: partly public; 1 mark: example explained [2]

items.stem: Residents of a street in Hanoi would all benefit from CCTV cameras, but nobody is willing to pay for them. Explain why.
items.answer: Each resident benefits whether or not they pay (non-excludable), so each waits for others to pay: the free rider problem.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: non-excludable; 1 mark: free riding [2]

items.stem: Residents of a street in Dubai would all benefit from CCTV cameras, but nobody is willing to pay for them. Explain why.
items.answer: Each resident benefits whether or not they pay (non-excludable), so each waits for others to pay: the free rider problem.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: non-excludable; 1 mark: free riding [2]

items.stem: A neighbourhood in Lisbon has 200 households. Each values a new set of street lights at $40. The lights would cost $4,000 to install. (a) Calculate the total value to the households and compare it with the cost. (b) Explain why the lights may not be provided by the market even though their value exceeds the cost. (c) Suggest how the lights could be provided.
items.answer: (a) Total value $8,000 > cost $4,000, so provision is worthwhile for society. (b) The lights are non-excludable: each household can free ride on others’ payments, so firms cannot collect enough revenue; a missing market. (c) Provision by the local council financed by taxes (or compulsory levy).
items.markingKey: (a) 200 × 40 = 8000 [1]; comparison [1] (b) non-excludable [1]; free rider/missing market [1] (c) government provision via taxation [1] [5]

(a) Calculate the percentage fall in the share of adults drinking sugary drinks daily. (b) Explain why sugary drinks may be classified as a demerit good.
items.answer: (a) 17.1% (b) Consumers underestimate the long-term health harm, so they over-consume relative to the optimum.
items.markingKey: (a) (35 − 29)/35 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Consumers underestimate the long-term health harm, so they over-consume relative to the optimum. [2]

items.stem: What is a merit good?
options: A good that wins awards for quality
A good that is more beneficial to consumers than they realise and is under-consumed in a free market
A good that is provided free by the government
items.answer: A good that is more beneficial to consumers than they realise and is under-consumed in a free market
items.markingKey: Merit goods: under-consumption due to information failure (and positive externalities).

items.stem: Explain why education is regarded as a merit good.
items.answer: Individuals, particularly the young, may underestimate the long-term benefits of education (higher lifetime earnings, better health), so in a free market it is under-consumed; there are also external benefits to society.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: benefits underestimated/information failure; 1 mark: under-consumed; 1 mark: external benefits [3]

items.stem: Explain how information failure leads to the over-consumption of demerit goods.
items.answer: Consumers underestimate the harm (to health, addiction) of goods such as cigarettes, so they buy more than they would with full information; consumption exceeds the socially optimal level.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: harm underestimated; 1 mark: over-consumption compared with full information [2]

items.stem: Cigarettes sold in Fendaria. How is this good best classified?
items.answer: Demerit good
items.markingKey: Demerit good: more harmful than consumers realise; over-consumed in a free market.

items.answer: Private good: excludable (pay to receive it) and rivalrous.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Private good; 1 mark: explanation – excludable (pay to receive it) and rivalrous. [2]

items.stem: Explain why the classification of goods as merit or demerit involves a value judgement.
items.answer: Deciding that people consume “too much” or “too little” of a good depends on views about what is good for them; individuals may disagree with the government.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: depends on judgement of what is beneficial; 1 mark: paternalism/consumers may disagree [2]

items.stem: The government of Sundara requires health warnings on packets of cigarettes. Explain how this could correct a market failure.
items.answer: Warnings give consumers better information about harm, reducing information failure, so demand falls towards the socially optimal level.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: improves information; 1 mark: demand falls [2]

items.stem: In a revision note Ana wrote: ‘Demerit goods are over-consumed because they are cheap.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: They are over-consumed mainly because consumers underestimate their harmful effects (information failure), whatever the price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – They are over-consumed mainly because consumers underestimate their harmful effects (information failure), whatever the price. [2]

items.stem: In Merania, 50% of children receive a flu vaccination when parents must pay $20. When the vaccination was made free in a trial region, take-up rose to 80%. The national child population is 200,000. (a) Calculate the cost to the government of free vaccinations nationally at the trial take-up rate, in millions of dollars. (b) Using the concept of a merit good, explain why take-up was low when parents paid. (c) Explain one reason why the policy may be worth its cost.
items.answer: (a) $3.2 million (b) Parents underestimate the benefits (information failure) and ignore benefits to others, so demand is below the social optimum. (c) External benefits: fewer infections in the wider population, lower healthcare costs and fewer days lost from work.
items.markingKey: (a) 200,000 × 80% × $20 = $3.2m [2] (b) information failure/under-consumption [1] (c) external benefits/savings [1] [4]

Because it is a public good
items.answer: It uses scarce resources that have alternative uses

items.stem: Explain why a good that has a zero price is not necessarily a free good.
items.answer: A zero price may be set by government or a firm, but if producing it uses scarce resources it has an opportunity cost and is an economic good.

items.stem: Zentara is considering whether to charge for the use of its main roads. Evaluate whether the government of Zentara should provide all public goods free of charge.

items.stem: What is the main reason merit goods are under-consumed in a free market?
options: Consumers lack full information about the benefits
Merit goods are always very expensive
Firms are unwilling to produce them
items.answer: Consumers lack full information about the benefits
items.markingKey: Information failure (imperfect information); short-termism.

items.stem: A student, Mohammed, claims: ‘A merit good is any good that is provided by the government.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: A merit good is one whose benefits are underestimated so it is under-consumed in a free market; it may be provided privately or publicly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A merit good is one whose benefits are underestimated so it is under-consumed in a free market; it may be provided privately or publicly. [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why education is regarded as a merit good. (b) Explain why the classification of goods as merit or demerit involves a value judgement.
items.answer: (a) Individuals, particularly the young, may underestimate the long-term benefits of education (higher lifetime earnings, better health), so in a free market it is under-consumed; there are also external benefits to society. (b) Deciding that people consume “too much” or “too little” of a good depends on views about what is good for them; individuals may disagree with the government.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: benefits underestimated/information failure; 1 mark: under-consumed; 1 mark: external benefits [3] (b) 1 mark: depends on judgement of what is beneficial; 1 mark: paternalism/consumers may disagree [2]

items.stem: In Merania, 60% of children receive a flu vaccination when parents must pay $20. When the vaccination was made free in a trial region, take-up rose to 85%. By how many percentage points did take-up rise?
items.answer: 25 percentage points

items.stem: Air breathed by people walking in a park in Cairo. How is this good best classified?
items.answer: Free good
items.markingKey: Free good: no resources are needed to provide it and there is no opportunity cost.

items.stem: Cigarettes sold in Marvona. How is this good best classified? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Demerit good: more harmful than consumers realise; over-consumed in a free market.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Demerit good; 1 mark: explanation – more harmful than consumers realise; over-consumed in a free market. [2]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Gorvania has introduced a 20% tax on sugary drinks and used the revenue to fund free fruit in primary schools and a new public park in Bangkok. The share of adults who drink sugary drinks daily fell from 28% to 24%. Some critics argue that people should be free to choose what they consume. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in the share of adults drinking sugary drinks daily. (b) Explain why sugary drinks may be classified as a demerit good.
items.answer: (a) 14.3% (b) Consumers underestimate the long-term health harm, so they over-consume relative to the optimum.
items.markingKey: (a) (28 − 24)/28 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Consumers underestimate the long-term health harm, so they over-consume relative to the optimum. [2]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Jovania has introduced a 25% tax on sugary drinks and used the revenue to fund free fruit in primary schools and a new public park in Doha. The share of adults who drink sugary drinks daily fell from 32% to 27%. Some critics argue that people should be free to choose what they consume. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in the share of adults drinking sugary drinks daily. (b) Explain why sugary drinks may be classified as a demerit good. (c) Explain why free fruit in schools may increase economic welfare.
items.answer: (a) 15.6% (b) Consumers underestimate the long-term health harm, so they over-consume relative to the optimum. (c) Merit good under-consumed due to information failure; free provision raises consumption; long-term health benefits.
items.markingKey: (a) (32 − 27)/32 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Consumers underestimate the long-term health harm, so they over-consume relative to the optimum. [2] (c) Credit: Merit good under-consumed due to information failure; free provision raises consumption; long-term health benefits. [2]
